---
abstract: |
  When several variables are observed over the same hierarchy, it seems natural to reconcile their forecasts jointly so that cross-variable dependence can inform the adjustment. We ask when joint reconciliation improves on reconciling each variable separately. Writing minimum trace reconciliation as a regression of the base forecast errors on the observed incoherences, we show that joint and separate reconciliation coincide if and only if each variable's separately reconciled errors are uncorrelated with the other variables' incoherences. This holds, for example, when the error covariance is separable or when the cross-variable dependence is confined to the coherent part of the errors. We propose two measures and a likelihood ratio test of this condition. In simulations, joint reconciliation reduces the mean squared error by at most `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$gainFtwoBrazilMax`% even when the true error covariance is known, and with an estimated covariance it is less accurate than separate reconciliation in small samples. We compare joint and separate reconciliation to monthly Brazilian employment admissions and dismissals over 2004--2019. With ARIMA base forecasts, joint reconciliation improves the forecasts of dismissals but not of admissions; with VAR base forecasts, it is worse than separate reconciliation for both. For net employment change, the difference between admissions and dismissals, joint reconciliation of the ARIMA forecasts reduces the national mean squared error by `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$appNetPointTotal`%. For probabilistic forecasts of net change, simulating the base forecasts jointly reduces the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$appNetJointSepTotal`%, and reconciling them jointly as well raises the reduction to `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$appNetJointJointTotal`%. Separate reconciliation is often sufficient for forecasting each variable, but the dependence between variables should be modelled when the quantity of interest combines them.
keywords:
  - hierarchical time series
  - coherent forecasts
  - minimum trace
  - Kronecker product
  - probabilistic forecasting
  - labour market
